memory_text: During Dashain, families gathered at the main house. Elders gave tika and jamara, and children walked across the village to receive blessings from relatives.
At Tihar we made a trail of oil lamps from the courtyard to the prayer room to welcome Laxmi. Sisters prepared garlands for Bhai Tika, and every household shared sel roti.
Gundruk began with mustard and radish leaves wilted in the sun, crushed tightly into an earthen pot, and sealed to ferment. After several days we dried it on a clean mat for winter soup.
Before sowing rice, we watched the flowering simal tree and listened for frogs after the first warm rain. Households exchanged seedlings so one failed nursery would not ruin a family's year.
Our village spring was said to appear where a tired traveller struck the earth with a walking stick. Nobody washed clothes at its source; the old story protected clean drinking water.
We say 'thuchi che' to offer thanks. Children learned to say it to people and quietly after receiving food or shelter, making gratitude an everyday habit.
Schoolchildren once wrote letters in fine dust spread across a wooden board before paper was common. Older pupils helped younger ones recite multiplication tables together beneath the pipal tree.
A bamboo doko is woven from the base upward. My father let my hands make loose crossings and then undid them with me; a strong basket came after learning not to fear beginning again.
